summary: Proposes a structured format for sending documents that mix several kinds of content, such as text and other media, between computer mail systems. It lays out how a document and its parts are described so different systems can exchange them.

plainLanguage.summary: Think of a lunch box with labeled compartments. This memo says how to pack text and other things into labeled sections so another computer knows what each part is.

questions: how to send multimedia documents by email in 1980
subtitle: A format for sending documents that mix text, images, fax, and voice through computer mail.

tldr.problem: Early message systems only supported plain text. As computers gained the ability to process graphics, facsimile, and digitized voice, there was no standard format for including these media types in messages.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 767 defines documents as property lists of named fields (DATE, SENDER, FROM, TO, SUBJECT, BODY, etc.) where the BODY can be simple text or a structured collection of multimedia elements with controlled presentation (sequential, simultaneous, or independent).
tldr.outcome: This format pioneered the concept of structured multimedia messages. Later standards like MIME adopted similar approaches for encoding attachments and mixed-media messages.

today: RFC 767 pioneered structured multimedia messaging. MIME (RFC 2045 onwards) later became the standard for encoding MIME-encoded message parts, using Content-Type headers rather than the property-list approach, but the fundamental concept of structured multimedia messages traces back to RFC 767.

sections.title: Multimedia Messages
sections.content:
RFC 767 specifies a format for transmitting structured data representations of multimedia documents using the Internet Message Protocol. As computer systems became capable of processing text, graphics, facsimile, and speech, the need arose for a standard way to encode these different media types in email messages.

The format is built on basic data elements used in the Internet Message Protocol and is flexible enough to accommodate new media types and features as they arise. The document structure is organized as fields (like DATE, SUBJECT, BODY) rather than the traditional header-and-body split, making it easier to extend with new field types.
sections.plainLanguage: Email used to be just text. Now we want to send pictures and voice too. This RFC shows a tidy way to package them together.

sections.title: Document Structure and Fields
sections.content:
A document is a property list of <name,value> pairs called fields. Required fields include DATE (in ISO format), SENDER (mailbox of the sender), SUBJECT (subject string), and BODY (the message content). Additional optional fields include FROM, TO, CC, BCC, REPLY-TO, and metadata fields like MESSAGE-ID, IN-REPLY-TO, KEYWORDS, and COMMENTS.

A mailbox field is itself a property list containing network, host, user name, person's real name, organization, and contact information. Distribution groups can be used to send a message to multiple recipients at once. Each field type has a defined structure that allows programs to parse and validate it automatically.
sections.plainLanguage: Each message is like a form with labeled blanks: who sent it, when, to whom, what the subject is, and then the content. Some blanks are required, others are optional.

sections.title: Multimedia Body Structures
sections.content:
The BODY field can be as simple as a single text string or as complex as a highly structured collection of different media types. Simple elements include just a text element. Structured text consists of paragraphs, each represented as text. Complex multimedia documents can combine text, graphics, facsimile, and voice in a presentation structure that specifies how they should be displayed: sequential (one after another), simultaneous (at the same time), or independent (in any order).

The RFC defines specific structures for graphics, facsimile, and voice, each with properties like format, protocol, encoding method, and resolution information. For example, graphics might specify TIFF or Postscript format, facsimile might specify Rapicom 450 or other formats, and voice might specify vocoder type and sampling rate.
sections.plainLanguage: The body can be just text, or text with pictures below it (sequential), or pictures and text shown together (simultaneous), or a reader picks which part to view (independent).

sections.title: Advanced Features
sections.content:
The format supports references to external data stored on remote hosts rather than embedding everything in the message. Pointers can specify network, host, filename, user credentials, and access instructions. This allows sending links to large files rather than entire file contents.

The RFC also provides for encoding and encryption. Documents can be partially or fully encrypted, and different media types may use different encryption schemes. A document can include NLS (oN-Line System) structured data from Douglas Engelbart's system, as NLS files were already tree-structured and could map naturally into the message format.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of sending a huge picture file in the email, you can send a link to it. You can also scramble the message so only the right person can read it.

references.text: Postel, J., "Internet Message Protocol", RFC 759, August 1980.
